topics.title: The Transformer Architecture & Attention
topics.description: Scaled Dot-Product Attention, Multi-Head Attention, RoPE, ALiBi, FlashAttention, and Encoder/Decoder architectures.

sections.title: The Transformer Architecture & Self-Attention
sections.subtitle: The Foundational Engine Powering Modern Generative AI and Foundation Models

sections.title: The Attention Breakthrough (Vaswani et al., 2017)
sections.text: Introduced in the landmark paper *Attention Is All You Need*, the **Transformer** abandoned recurrent and convolutional connections entirely, relying solely on **Self-Attention** mechanisms. In self-attention, each token in a sequence directly computes pairwise interactions with every other token, capturing long-range contextual relationships with an $O(1)$ sequential path length and enabling massive parallel training on modern GPU clusters.

sections.title: Scaled Dot-Product Attention Formula
sections.text:
Given packed matrices for Queries ($Q$), Keys ($K$), and Values ($V$), where $Q, K \in \mathbb{R}^{T \times d_k}$ and $V \in \mathbb{R}^{T \times d_v}$:

$$\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\left( \frac{Q K^T}{\sqrt{d_k}} + M \right) V$$

- **Scaling Factor $\sqrt{d_k}$:** Prevents dot products from growing excessively large in high dimensions, which would push softmax into flat regions with vanishing gradients.
- **Mask Matrix $M$:** In autoregressive decoder models (e.g. GPT), an upper-triangular causal mask of $-\infty$ prevents positions from attending to future tokens.

sections.title: Transformer Architecture Paradigms
rows: Encoder-Only
Bidirectional Attention (all tokens attend to all tokens).
BERT, RoBERTa, DeBERTa
Deep bidirectional contextual representations.
Classification, Named Entity Recognition, Extractive QA, Embeddings.
Decoder-Only
Causal / Autoregressive Attention (tokens only attend to past tokens).
GPT-4, Llama 3, Mistral, Claude
Unbounded generative continuation, seamless zero-shot prompting.
Conversational agents, code generation, creative writing, reasoning.
Encoder-Decoder
Bidirectional Encoder + Causal Cross-Attention Decoder.
T5, BART, Original 2017 Transformer
Maps source sequence to arbitrary target sequence.
Machine translation, document summarization, question answering.

sections.title: Modern Positional Embeddings: RoPE & ALiBi
sections.text:
1. **Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE, Su et al., 2021):** Encodes absolute positions with a rotation matrix that naturally preserves relative positional distances in inner products: $q_m^T k_n = g(x_m, x_n, m - n)$. Standard in Llama, Mistral, and Gemma.
2. **ALiBi (Attention with Linear Biases, Press et al., 2022):** Injects a static linear bias penalty proportional to token distance $|i - j|$ directly into attention logits, enabling zero-shot context length extrapolation.

sections.title: FlashAttention (Dao et al., 2022-2024)
sections.body: Standard attention materializes an $O(N^2)$ attention matrix in high-bandwidth memory (HBM), creating a major memory bandwidth bottleneck. **FlashAttention** reorganizes the computation using tiling to compute softmax incrementally (online softmax) entirely within fast GPU SRAM without ever writing the full $N \times N$ intermediate attention matrix to HBM, achieving a **2x-4x speedup** and reducing memory from $O(N^2)$ to $O(N)$.

code_example.title: Vectorized Multi-Head Self-Attention in NumPy
code_example.code:
import numpy as np

def softmax(x, axis=-1):
    e_x = np.exp(x - np.max(x, axis=axis, keepdims=True))
    return e_x / np.sum(e_x, axis=axis, keepdims=True)

def multi_head_attention(X, W_q, W_k, W_v, W_o, num_heads=2, causal_mask=True):
    # X: (T, d_model)
    T, d_model = X.shape
    d_k = d_model // num_heads
    
    # 1. Project into Q, K, V
    Q = np.dot(X, W_q).reshape(T, num_heads, d_k).transpose(1, 0, 2) # (H, T, d_k)
    K = np.dot(X, W_k).reshape(T, num_heads, d_k).transpose(1, 0, 2)
    V = np.dot(X, W_v).reshape(T, num_heads, d_k).transpose(1, 0, 2)
    
    # 2. Scaled Dot-Product Attention: (H, T, T)
    scores = np.matmul(Q, K.transpose(0, 2, 1)) / np.sqrt(d_k)
    
    if causal_mask:
        mask = np.triu(np.ones((T, T)), k=1)
        scores = np.where(mask == 1, -1e9, scores)
        
    attn_weights = softmax(scores, axis=-1)
    context = np.matmul(attn_weights, V) # (H, T, d_k)
    
    # 3. Concatenate heads and project
    context = context.transpose(1, 0, 2).reshape(T, d_model)
    output = np.dot(context, W_o)
    return output, attn_weights

# Test forward pass with T=4 tokens, d_model=8, 2 heads
np.random.seed(42)
T, d_model = 4, 8
X = np.random.randn(T, d_model)
W_q = np.random.randn(d_model, d_model) * 0.2
W_k = np.random.randn(d_model, d_model) * 0.2
W_v = np.random.randn(d_model, d_model) * 0.2
W_o = np.random.randn(d_model, d_model) * 0.2

out, weights = multi_head_attention(X, W_q, W_k, W_v, W_o, num_heads=2, causal_mask=True)
print(f'Multi-Head Output Shape: {out.shape}')
print('Head 0 Attention Weights (Causal Lower Triangular):')
print(np.round(weights[0], 3))

quiz.question: Who authored the foundational paper 'Attention Is All You Need' in 2017?
options: Vaswani et al. (Google Brain / Google Research)
LeCun, Bengio, and Hinton
Radford et al. (OpenAI)
Devlin et al.
quiz.explanation: Ashish Vaswani and seven Google colleagues published 'Attention Is All You Need' at NeurIPS 2017.

quiz.question: What is the computational complexity of standard self-attention with respect to sequence length N?
options: O(N)
O(N log N)
quiz.explanation: Computing pairwise dot products between all N queries and N keys forms an N x N matrix, scaling quadratically O(N^2).

quiz.question: Why is the dot product Q * K^T scaled by 1 / sqrt(d_k) in Scaled Dot-Product Attention?
options: To prevent the magnitude of dot products from growing large for large d_k, which pushes softmax into saturated regions with near-zero gradients
To ensure positive eigenvalues
To eliminate the need for bias terms
To make attention symmetric
quiz.explanation: For independent zero-mean unit-variance variables, the dot product has variance d_k; dividing by sqrt(d_k) restores variance to 1, preventing softmax saturation.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of the causal mask (upper triangular -inf mask) in autoregressive decoders like GPT?
options: To prevent token t from attending to future tokens t+1, t+2... during training, enforcing strict left-to-right autoregressive causality
To mask out profanity
To remove stop words
To compress model weights
quiz.explanation: Setting upper-triangular logits to -inf forces their softmax weights to exactly zero, guaranteeing tokens can only attend to past and present positions.

quiz.question: How does Multi-Head Attention benefit the model compared to a single attention head of the same total dimension?
options: It allows the model to jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions simultaneously
It multiplies the number of parameters by the number of heads
It eliminates the need for feedforward layers
It guarantees zero training error
quiz.explanation: Multiple heads project representations into distinct subspaces, allowing head 1 to track syntactic agreement while head 2 tracks semantic coreference.

quiz.question: Why do Transformers require Positional Encodings / Embeddings?
options: Because self-attention is strictly permutation-equivariant; without positional information, the model treats a sequence as an unordered bag of tokens
To compress long sentences into one vector
To calculate cross-entropy loss
To initialize weights
quiz.explanation: Attention computes set-level dot products without inherent order; positional embeddings inject spatial sequence information.

quiz.question: What is Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE, Su et al., 2021)?
options: A relative positional encoding method that applies a 2D rotation matrix to query and key vectors in the complex plane, decaying dot product with relative distance
A method that rotates weights by 90 degrees
A positional encoding for robotic arms
A random shuffle of token positions
quiz.explanation: RoPE encodes relative position directly into Q and K via complex rotation, allowing seamless relative distance decay across long sequences.

quiz.question: What is ALiBi (Attention with Linear Biases, Press et al., 2022)?
options: Subtracting a static linear penalty m * |i - j| from attention logits before softmax, enabling zero-shot context extrapolation beyond training length
A deep linear neural network
A loss function for adversarial attacks
A method for pruning linear layers
quiz.explanation: ALiBi adds a non-learned linear penalty proportional to token distance directly to attention logits, achieving remarkable length extrapolation.

quiz.question: What is FlashAttention (Dao et al., 2022)?
options: An IO-aware exact attention algorithm that tiles computation to operate within fast GPU SRAM using online softmax, avoiding writing the N x N attention matrix to HBM
An approximate linear attention method
A 4-bit quantization library
A tool for flash memory storage
quiz.explanation: FlashAttention avoids GPU High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM) memory bottlenecks by fusing attention into SRAM tiles, yielding 2-4x wall-clock speedups with exact math.

quiz.question: What is FlashAttention-2 (Dao, 2023)?
options: An optimized version that reduces non-matmul FLOPs, optimizes work partitioning across thread blocks, and achieves up to 73% theoretical GPU FLOP utilization
A model with half the parameters
A pruned attention module
A tool for mobile devices
quiz.explanation: FlashAttention-2 refines thread block scheduling and online softmax scaling, running significantly closer to the theoretical maximum TFLOPs of A100/H100 GPUs.

quiz.question: What is Multi-Query Attention (MQA, Shazeer, 2019)?
options: An attention variant where all attention heads share a single common Key and Value head while retaining separate Query heads, reducing KV cache memory during inference
Using multiple search queries simultaneously
An attention head with multiple outputs
A query optimization for SQL databases
quiz.explanation: MQA shares one K and one V projection across all H query heads, drastically reducing KV cache size and memory bandwidth pressure during autoregressive generation.

quiz.question: What is Grouped-Query Attention (GQA, Ainslie et al., 2023)?
options: An attention mechanism that groups query heads (e.g. 8 groups) and assigns one K and V head per group, interpolating between standard MHA and MQA
Grouping queries by topic
A cluster of GPUs running attention
A batching algorithm for text
quiz.explanation: GQA (used in Llama 2/3 and Mistral) strikes an optimal trade-off between full MHA quality and MQA speed/memory efficiency.

quiz.question: What is the Key-Value (KV) Cache in autoregressive Transformer generation?
options: Storing past keys and values in GPU memory so each new generated token only needs to compute queries for itself rather than recomputing all past tokens
A caching server using Redis
A cache for tokenizer lookups
A method to store model checkpoints
quiz.explanation: During autoregressive inference, past tokens do not change; caching their K and V representations avoids O(T^2) redundant computation per token.

quiz.question: What is PagedAttention (Kwon et al., vLLM 2023)?
options: Managing the KV cache like virtual memory with non-contiguous memory pages, eliminating memory fragmentation and boosting serving throughput by 2x-4x
Splitting text into book pages
Paging memory to hard disk
A paper reading algorithm
quiz.explanation: Inspired by OS virtual memory paging, PagedAttention stores KV cache in allocated non-contiguous memory blocks, eliminating internal fragmentation and enabling efficient memory sharing.

quiz.question: What is the Feed-Forward Network (FFN) layer inside a Transformer block typically composed of?
options: Two linear projections with an intermediate non-linear expansion (typically 4x hidden dimension), e.g., W_2 * GELU(W_1 * x + b_1) + b_2
A single convolutional layer
An LSTM cell
A softmax layer
quiz.explanation: The standard Transformer MLP expands representations to 4 * d_model (or 8/3 with SwiGLU) with non-linear activation before projecting back to d_model.

quiz.question: What is the SwiGLU activation function (Shazeer, 2020), widely adopted in modern LLMs?
options: A gated linear unit variant: SwiGLU(x) = (x W_1 * Swish(x W_gate)) W_2
A mix of Sigmoid and ReLU
A sinusoidal activation
A step function with glue
quiz.explanation: SwiGLU combines Swish (SiLU) with a multiplicative gating branch, empirically outperforming standard ReLU and GELU across modern architectures (Llama, PaLM).

quiz.question: What is the role of the Residual Stream in a Transformer?
options: The central communication backbone where each attention and MLP layer reads from and writes updates to via additive skip connections
A stream of input tokens from disk
A backup system for crashed runs
A buffer for discarded gradients
quiz.explanation: The residual stream carries representations throughout the model; layers act as read-write heads that add deltas to this shared representation highway.

quiz.question: What is the difference between Pre-LayerNorm (Pre-LN) and Post-LayerNorm (Post-LN)?
options: Pre-LN applies normalization to layer inputs before attention/FFN; Post-LN normalizes after the residual addition
Pre-LN normalizes the dataset before training
Post-LN is only used in vision
Pre-LN requires no parameters
quiz.explanation: Pre-LN (used in GPT-2, Llama) ensures an unhindered identity residual stream, eliminating the training instability of the original Vaswani Post-LN.

quiz.question: What is Cross-Attention in an Encoder-Decoder Transformer?
options: Queries come from the decoder's previous layer, while Keys and Values come from the encoder's final output representations
Attention calculated between two different models
Queries and keys are crossed randomly
Attention across multiple GPUs
quiz.explanation: Cross-attention enables the decoder to condition on the encoded source sequence by matching decoder queries against encoder keys and values.

quiz.question: What type of Transformer architecture is BERT (Devlin et al., 2018)?
options: Encoder-only architecture with bidirectional attention
Decoder-only autoregressive architecture
Encoder-decoder Seq2Seq model
Recurrent neural network
quiz.explanation: BERT consists strictly of Transformer encoder blocks, utilizing unmasked bidirectional attention across all positions.

quiz.question: What type of Transformer architecture is the GPT series (Radford et al., OpenAI)?
options: Decoder-only autoregressive architecture with causal masking
Encoder-only bidirectional model
Encoder-decoder model
Graph neural network
quiz.explanation: GPT models use Transformer decoder blocks without cross-attention, using causal self-attention to generate tokens autoregressively.

quiz.question: What type of Transformer architecture is T5 (Raffel et al., Google 2020)?
options: Full Encoder-Decoder architecture formulating every NLP problem as a text-to-text task
Decoder-only
Encoder-only
Convolutional backbone
quiz.explanation: T5 employs an encoder-decoder architecture where both input and output are treated as text sequences.

quiz.question: What is a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Transformer (e.g. Mixtral 8x7B, Switch Transformer)?
options: Replacing dense FFN layers with multiple expert FFN sub-networks and using a learned router to direct each token to top-K experts per layer
Using an ensemble of 8 completely separate models
Consulting human experts during inference
A model trained on 8 languages
quiz.explanation: MoE scales parameter capacity to tens or hundreds of billions while keeping inference compute (FLOPs per token) fixed by selectively routing tokens to a subset of experts.

quiz.question: What is the router (gating network) in a Mixture-of-Experts layer?
options: A parameterized linear softmax classifier that computes routing probability scores over experts for each token
A physical internet network router
A hash function that distributes tokens randomly
A script that loads weights from disk
quiz.explanation: The gating network computes G(x) = Softmax(TopK(x * W_g)), routing each token vector dynamically to the K highest scoring expert networks.

quiz.question: What is 'Expert Collapse' in Mixture-of-Experts training, and how is it prevented?
options: When the router routes all tokens to the same 1 or 2 experts while leaving others untrained; prevented using an auxiliary load-balancing loss
When the model crashes due to lack of RAM
When weights decay to zero
When experts disagree on predictions
quiz.explanation: Auxiliary load-balancing losses penalize uneven expert assignment, ensuring all expert networks receive a balanced distribution of training tokens.

quiz.question: What is Context Length Extrapolation in LLMs?
options: The ability of a model trained on context length L (e.g. 4k tokens) to evaluate and generate coherently on longer sequences (e.g. 32k tokens)
Writing longer prompts
Increasing model size by 8x
Translating into longer languages
quiz.explanation: Extrapolation refers to evaluating sequences longer than the maximum position indices encountered during training without performance collapse.

quiz.question: What is Linear RoPE Scaling / YaRN for context length extension?
options: Scaling down positional frequencies in RoPE to compress longer sequence positions into the frequency range observed during pretraining
Doubling the learning rate
Padding the context with spaces
Removing 50% of the attention heads
quiz.explanation: Interpolating positional frequencies allows pretrained models to extend their context window from 4k to 32k or 128k with minimal fine-tuning.

quiz.question: What is Sliding Window Attention (used in Mistral 7B)?
options: Each token attends only to the W previous tokens (e.g. W=4096) at each layer, reducing attention cost from O(N^2) to O(N * W)
Opening multiple browser windows
Sliding the entire dataset across GPUs
Moving average of weights
quiz.explanation: Sliding window attention restricts the receptive field per layer to W tokens, while multi-layer stacking still achieves a receptive field of L * W.

quiz.question: What is the theoretical maximum receptive field of a stacked L-layer Transformer using Sliding Window Attention with window size W?
options: L * W
W
L + W
W^L
quiz.explanation: Information propagates by W tokens at each layer, so L stacked layers achieve an effective context receptive field of L * W.

quiz.question: What is Speculative Decoding (Leviathan et al., 2023 / Chen et al., 2023)?
options: Using a small, fast draft model to generate K candidate tokens, then verifying all K tokens in a single parallel forward pass of the large target model
Guessing future stock market prices with an LLM
Generating text with random temperature
Training without a loss function
quiz.explanation: Speculative decoding accelerates inference latency by 2x-3x without altering the target model's output probability distribution.

quiz.question: What is KV Cache Compression (e.g., StreamingLLM, H2O)?
options: Retaining only critical attention sinks (initial tokens) and recent sliding window tokens in the KV cache, enabling infinite-length generation without running out of VRAM
Compressing KV cache with zip
Quantizing embeddings to 1 bit
Discarding all keys
quiz.explanation: Xiao et al. showed that keeping the first 4 'attention sink' tokens plus the recent window allows stable autoregressive streaming without memory explosion.

quiz.question: Why do Transformer models exhibit 'Attention Sinks' at the very first tokens?
options: Because softmax must sum to 1, early tokens act as a dumping ground for unnecessary attention score mass even if they have no semantic relevance
Because the first token is always the title
Because of GPU memory alignment
Because of zero padding
quiz.explanation: Softmax requires attention weights to sum to 1 across all positions; tokens with nothing useful to attend to dump their attention mass into initial tokens.

quiz.question: What is Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) Masked LM objective?
options: Masking 15% of input tokens with a [MASK] token and training the model to predict the original tokens using bidirectional context
Hiding the entire input sequence
Masking out attention matrices
Predicting the next word in a sentence
quiz.explanation: MLM masks random tokens and optimizes cross-entropy on predicting the masked vocabulary IDs given bidirectional surrounding context.

quiz.question: What is the difference between extractive QA and abstractive QA in language modeling?
options: Extractive QA extracts the exact answer span directly from the provided passage; abstractive QA synthesizes a fluent original answer in natural language
Extractive QA uses regex only
Abstractive QA is only for math problems
They are identical
quiz.explanation: Extractive models (like BERT for SQuAD) output start and end token indices; abstractive models (like GPT) generate free-form text.

quiz.question: How does Vision Transformer (ViT, Dosovitskiy et al., 2020) process an image as a sequence of tokens?
options: By splitting the image into non-overlapping patches (e.g. 16x16 pixels), linearly projecting each patch into an embedding vector, and treating them as sequence tokens
By feeding one pixel at a time into an RNN
By running a CNN first to find edges
By converting the image to audio
quiz.explanation: ViT breaks an image into a grid of 16x16 patches, flattens them, applies a linear projection, adds positional embeddings, and feeds them into a standard Transformer encoder.

topics.description: Subword Tokenization (BPE, WordPiece, SentencePiece), Byte-Level BPE, Embedding spaces, and Pretraining Objectives.

sections.title: Modern NLP Pipelines & Subword Tokenization
sections.subtitle: From Raw Unicode Text to Discrete Subword Vocabularies and High-Dimensional Embeddings

sections.title: The Fundamental Tokenization Trade-Off
sections.text:
Machine learning models process numbers, not strings. Tokenization bridges this gap:
- **Word-Level Tokenization:** Suffers from massive vocabularies ($> 500,000$ words) and cannot handle Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) words or rare morphological variations (e.g., *unfriendliness* $\to$ `<UNK>`).
- **Character-Level Tokenization:** Zero OOV issues with a tiny vocabulary (~256 tokens), but sequences become excessively long ($5\times$ longer), crippling self-attention which scales as $O(N^2)$.
- **Subword Tokenization (BPE / WordPiece / SentencePiece):** The gold standard. Decomposes rare words into frequent subword units while keeping common words intact, achieving compact vocabularies ($32,000 - 128,000$ tokens) with zero OOV tokens.

sections.title: Subword Tokenization Algorithms Compared
rows: Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE)
Iteratively merges the most frequent adjacent pair of symbols in the training corpus.
Requires pre-tokenization (e.g., regex splitting on spaces).
Original BPE (Sennrich, 2016), GPT-2 / GPT-4 (Byte-level BPE).
WordPiece
Iteratively merges the symbol pair that maximizes the likelihood of the training corpus under a unigram language model (maximizing $\frac{\text{count}(ab)}{\text{count}(a)\text{count}(b)}$).
Uses prefix markers (e.g., `##ing`) for continuation subwords.
BERT, DistilBERT, Electra.
Unigram Language Model
Starts with a massive seed vocabulary and iteratively prunes the 20% of subwords whose removal increases corpus perplexity least.
Treats text as a raw stream; uses `_` to denote spaces.
SentencePiece (Kudo, 2018), T5, ALBERT, LLaMA.
Byte-Level BPE (BBPE)
Operates on raw UTF-8 bytes ($256$ base tokens) instead of Unicode characters.
Can encode any arbitrary character, emoji, or binary byte without `<UNK>`.
GPT-2, GPT-3, GPT-4, Llama 2/3, Mistral.

sections.title: BPE Merge Algorithm Walkthrough
sections.text:
Given a corpus of words with end-of-word markers:
`{'l o w </w>': 5, 'l o w e s t </w>': 2, 'n e w e r </w>': 6, 'w i d e r </w>': 3}`

1. Count all adjacent symbol pairs across the corpus.
2. Most frequent pair: `('e', 'r')` appearing $6 + 3 = 9$ times.
3. Merge into new token `'er'` $\to$ vocabulary gains `'er'`.
4. Repeat for $K$ merge operations until target vocabulary size is reached.

sections.title: Pretraining Objectives: Causal vs Masked vs Span Corruption
sections.body:
- **Causal Language Modeling (CLM):** Next-token prediction: $\max_\theta \sum_{t=1}^T \log P(x_t \mid x_{<t}; \theta)$. Powers all modern generative autoregressive LLMs.
- **Masked Language Modeling (MLM):** Predicts randomly masked tokens ($15\%$) given both left and right context: $\max_\theta \sum_{i \in \mathcal{M}} \log P(x_i \mid \tilde{X}; \theta)$. Powers BERT.
- **Span Corruption:** Replaces random multi-token spans with sentinel tokens (e.g. `<extra_id_0>`) and decodes only the missing spans. Powers Google T5.

code_example.title: Implementing Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) Learner from Scratch
code_example.code:
import collections

def get_stats(vocab):
    pairs = collections.defaultdict(int)
    for word, freq in vocab.items():
        symbols = word.split()
        for i in range(len(symbols) - 1):
            pairs[symbols[i], symbols[i + 1]] += freq
    return pairs

def merge_vocab(pair, v_in):
    v_out = {}
    bigram = ' '.join(pair)
    replacement = ''.join(pair)
    for word in v_in:
        # Replace adjacent pair
        w_out = word.replace(bigram, replacement)
        v_out[w_out] = v_in[word]
    return v_out

# Toy corpus
vocab = {
    'l o w </w>': 5,
    'l o w e s t </w>': 2,
    'n e w e r </w>': 6,
    'w i d e r </w>': 3,
    'n e w </w>': 2
}

print('Initial Vocabulary Counts:', vocab)
num_merges = 5

for i in range(num_merges):
    pairs = get_stats(vocab)
    if not pairs: break
    best_pair = max(pairs, key=pairs.get)
    vocab = merge_vocab(best_pair, vocab)
    print(f'Merge {i+1}: Best Pair {best_pair} (Freq: {pairs[best_pair]}) -> New Vocab sample: {list(vocab.keys())[0]}')

print('\nFinal Learned Representation:', vocab)

quiz.question: Why is subword tokenization preferred over pure word-level tokenization in modern NLP?
options: It avoids Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) errors by decomposing unseen words into known subwords while maintaining a compact vocabulary size
It guarantees 100% classification accuracy
It reduces network depth to 1 layer
It eliminates the need for embeddings
quiz.explanation: Subword tokenizers decompose unknown or rare words (e.g. 'unprecedentedly' -> 'un', 'precedent', 'ed', 'ly') into recognized sub-units without `<UNK>`.

quiz.question: Why is subword tokenization preferred over pure character-level tokenization?
options: Character-level tokenization results in 4x-6x longer sequences, which quadruples or octuples computational memory due to O(N^2) attention complexity
Characters cannot be represented in UTF-8
Characters have no mathematical embeddings
Character models cannot generate punctuation
quiz.explanation: Attention scales quadratically with sequence length; character tokenization makes sequences so long that training becomes computationally prohibitive.

quiz.question: How does Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) build its vocabulary during the training phase?
options: By iteratively counting adjacent symbol pairs in the corpus and merging the single most frequent pair into a new subword token
By randomly picking words from a dictionary
By splitting words alphabetically
By training a decision tree on text
quiz.explanation: BPE starts with all individual characters and iteratively merges the most frequent co-occurring adjacent symbol pairs until reaching the target vocabulary size.

quiz.question: What is Byte-Level BPE (BBPE), used in GPT-2, GPT-4, and LLaMA?
options: Running BPE over the 256 possible base bytes of raw UTF-8 rather than Unicode characters, allowing any text, code, or emoji to be tokenized without <UNK>
A tokenizer that only handles numbers
A tokenizer that compresses text with gzip
A tokenizer with only 8 tokens
quiz.explanation: By treating raw bytes as the base alphabet, Byte-Level BPE can represent any arbitrary Unicode character, symbol, or binary file without out-of-vocabulary tokens.

quiz.question: How does WordPiece tokenization differ from BPE in its merge selection criterion?
options: WordPiece merges the symbol pair that maximizes the likelihood of the training data under a language model, rather than purely picking the most frequent pair
WordPiece splits words by length
WordPiece only works on Chinese text
WordPiece uses negative frequencies
quiz.explanation: WordPiece scores candidates by how much adding the pair increases the corpus likelihood relative to the individual symbol probabilities.

quiz.question: What does the `##` prefix indicate in BERT's WordPiece tokenizer (e.g. `affable` -> `aff`, `##able`)?
options: It indicates that `##able` is a continuation subword attached to the previous token, not a standalone word
It indicates a comment in code
It indicates a hashtag
It indicates an invalid character
quiz.explanation: WordPiece prepends `##` to continuation fragments so the model knows the subword does not start a new word.

quiz.question: What is SentencePiece (Kudo, 2018)?
options: An unsupervised text tokenizer that treats raw text as a sequence of Unicode characters without requiring language-dependent whitespace pre-tokenization
A tool for counting grammatical sentences
A parser for sentence syntax trees
A spell-checker for English
quiz.explanation: SentencePiece treats whitespace as a regular character (`_`), allowing completely lossless tokenization across languages that do not use whitespace (e.g. Japanese, Chinese).

quiz.question: What is the Unigram Language Model tokenization algorithm (Kudo, 2018)?
options: Starting with a large seed vocabulary and iteratively pruning subwords that cause the smallest increase in corpus perplexity until reaching target vocabulary size
An algorithm that only uses single-letter words
A model that never merges tokens
A method for training n-gram grammars
quiz.explanation: Unigram tokenization starts with a huge dictionary and prunes subwords that contribute least to corpus likelihood, offering probabilistic subword segmentations.

quiz.question: What is Tokenizer 'Vocabulary Size' (Vocab Size)?
options: The total number of unique discrete token IDs that the model recognizes and maps to embedding vectors
The number of words in the user's prompt
The file size of the tokenizer in megabytes
The number of layers in the model
quiz.explanation: Vocab size represents the total entries in the embedding table (e.g. 32,000 in LLaMA, 50,257 in GPT-2, 100,000 in GPT-4, 256,000 in Gemma).

quiz.question: What is the trade-off of having a very large vocabulary size (e.g. 256,000 vs 32,000)?
options: A larger vocabulary produces shorter sequence lengths (fewer tokens per sentence) but consumes significantly more parameter memory in the input/output embedding matrices
A large vocabulary eliminates the need for attention
A large vocabulary slows down token generation to 1 token/min
A large vocabulary cannot handle punctuation
quiz.explanation: Larger vocabularies compress text into fewer tokens, speeding up self-attention, but require massive embedding tables (e.g. 256k * 4096 params = 1B params just for embeddings).

quiz.question: What is 'Tokenization Glitch' or 'SolidGoldMagikarp' phenomenon in LLMs?
options: Anomalous tokens in the vocabulary that appeared frequently in pretraining web crawls but were never exposed to gradient updates during instruction tuning, causing bizarre model behaviors
A bug in the Pokemon video game
A memory leak in CUDA
A corrupted GPU cache
quiz.explanation: Certain tokens (like Reddit usernames) had dedicated vocabulary IDs with uncalibrated embedding vectors, causing erratic outputs when prompted.

quiz.question: What is Causal Language Modeling (CLM) pretraining objective?
options: Predicting the next token given all prior tokens in the sequence: P(x_t | x_1, ..., x_{t-1})
Predicting whether text is true or false
Predicting the middle token given left and right context
Classifying the sentiment of a sentence
quiz.explanation: CLM trains models to minimize cross-entropy loss on predicting token t given tokens 1 through t-1, powering all autoregressive LLMs.

quiz.question: What is Masked Language Modeling (MLM) pretraining objective?
options: Randomly masking out a portion of tokens (typically 15%) and training the model to predict the masked tokens using bidirectional context
Masking the entire output sentence
Predicting future stock prices
Removing consonants from words
quiz.explanation: MLM allows deep bidirectional feature representations by predicting masked tokens from both preceding and succeeding context.

quiz.question: What was the Next Sentence Prediction (NSP) objective in the original BERT model?
options: A binary classification task predicting whether sentence B immediately follows sentence A in the original text
Predicting the word count of the next sentence
Translating the next sentence to French
Summarizing the next paragraph
quiz.explanation: BERT used NSP to help the model learn inter-sentence relationships, though subsequent models (RoBERTa) proved NSP was largely unnecessary.

quiz.question: Why did RoBERTa (Liu et al., 2019) outperform original BERT?
options: It removed the Next Sentence Prediction task, trained on 10x more data with dynamic masking, larger mini-batches, and longer sequences
It switched to an RNN architecture
It used half the parameters
It used a 4-bit integer tokenizer
quiz.explanation: RoBERTa demonstrated that BERT was severely undertrained, and removing NSP while scaling data and batch size yielded substantial gains.

quiz.question: What is Span Corruption pretraining (used in T5)?
options: Replacing variable-length continuous spans of text with sentinel tokens (<extra_id_0>) and training the decoder to reconstruct only the deleted spans
Corrupting memory spans in GPU VRAM
Deleting random files from disk
Scrambling the order of sentences
quiz.explanation: T5's span corruption masks consecutive spans of ~3 tokens and trains an encoder-decoder to generate the missing masked spans.

quiz.question: What is Word2Vec (Mikolov et al., 2013)?
options: A shallow 2-layer neural model that learns dense distributed vector representations of words based on local context windows via CBOW or Skip-Gram
A dictionary lookup algorithm
A rule-based linguistic parser
A document translation tool
quiz.explanation: Word2Vec revolutionized NLP by producing dense vectors where geometric proximity and vector arithmetic (King - Man + Woman = Queen) captured semantic relationships.

quiz.question: How does the Continuous Bag of Words (CBOW) architecture differ from Skip-Gram in Word2Vec?
options: CBOW predicts the target word from surrounding context words; Skip-Gram predicts the surrounding context words given the target word
CBOW is bidirectional; Skip-Gram is unidirectional
CBOW only works on verbs
Skip-Gram uses convolutional filters
quiz.explanation: CBOW averages context words to predict the center word; Skip-Gram uses the center word to predict its neighborhood context words.

quiz.question: What was the fundamental limitation of static word embeddings like Word2Vec and GloVe?
options: They assigned a single fixed vector to each word regardless of context, unable to handle polysemy (e.g. 'bank' of a river vs financial 'bank')
They required 100 GPUs to train
They only worked on binary numbers
They could not calculate cosine similarity
quiz.explanation: Static embeddings cannot disambiguate polysemous words; contextual models (ELMo, BERT) dynamically alter embeddings based on surrounding syntax and semantics.

quiz.question: What is an Embedding Lookup Table mathematically in a neural network?
options: A matrix multiplication with a one-hot encoded vector: x_embed = one_hot(token_id) * E
A hash table stored on disk
A binary search tree
A random number generator
quiz.explanation: Retrieving row i from an embedding table E is mathematically equivalent to multiplying the one-hot representation of token i by the weight matrix E.

quiz.question: What is Weight Tying (Press & Wolf, 2017) between input and output embeddings?
options: Sharing the exact same weight matrix for the input token embedding layer and the final pre-softmax output projection layer
Tying weights with an elastic regularization rope
Tying the weights of layer 1 to layer 10
Freezing all weights to 1.0
quiz.explanation: Weight tying reuses the input embedding matrix as the final linear projection matrix, slashing model parameter counts by tens of millions of weights with zero loss in accuracy.

quiz.question: What is 'Lossless Tokenization' in modern tokenizers?
options: The ability to perfectly reconstruct the exact original input string (including whitespaces and capitalization) from its token IDs: decode(encode(text)) == text
A tokenizer that uses zero bytes of memory
A tokenizer that never drops tokens
A tokenizer that does not use loss functions
quiz.explanation: Lossless tokenization ensures that formatting, whitespace, indentation in code, and punctuation are preserved with 100% fidelity across encode/decode roundtrips.

quiz.question: What is Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) rate?
options: The percentage of tokens in a dataset that do not exist in the tokenizer's vocabulary and must be mapped to the unknown <UNK> token
The rate at which vocabulary files are downloaded
The number of misspelled words in a dictionary
The loss of the tokenizer
quiz.explanation: A high OOV rate indicates poor tokenizer coverage; modern subword/byte-level tokenizers achieve an OOV rate of 0%.

quiz.question: What is the effect of tokenizing code with a tokenizer trained only on English prose?
options: Code becomes severely fragmented into many tiny tokens (individual characters or 2-letter fragments), inflating sequence length and hurting model comprehension
The model converts code to English
The code runs 10x faster
The compiler throws a syntax error
quiz.explanation: Without specialized programming tokens (like indentation spaces, operators, syntax keywords), sequence lengths blow up, consuming massive context budgets.

quiz.question: Why do modern LLM tokenizers (like GPT-4's cl100k_base or LLaMA 3's 128k tokenizer) include dedicated tokens for runs of spaces (e.g. '    ' 4 spaces)?
options: To compress code indentation into single tokens, significantly reducing sequence length and boosting coding performance
To save hard drive space
To remove blank lines
To make text look aligned
quiz.explanation: In Python and codebases, 4-space indentations occur millions of times; dedicating single token IDs to repeated whitespace drastically cuts sequence lengths.

quiz.question: What is a 'Special Token' in NLP vocabularies (e.g. `[CLS]`, `[SEP]`, `<|endoftext|>`)?
options: Reserved tokens with dedicated IDs that designate structural signals like sentence boundaries, sequence starts, or document termination
A token with a higher learning rate
A token encrypted for security
A token that prints emojis
quiz.explanation: Special tokens act as architectural control markers: `[CLS]` aggregates sequence representations, and `<|endoftext|>` signals generation completion.

quiz.question: What is Truncation and Padding in batch text processing?
options: Padding adds pad tokens to shorter sequences to equalize lengths in a batch; truncation cuts sequences that exceed the maximum length limit
Compressing files with zip
Deleting negative numbers
Rotating text tensors
quiz.explanation: Batches require uniform tensor dimensions (Batch_Size, Max_Length); padding fills vacant slots, and truncation bounds excessive lengths.

quiz.question: What is an Attention Mask in Transformer text processing?
options: A binary tensor indicating which tokens are real content (1) and should be attended to, versus which tokens are padding (0) and must be ignored
A mask worn by researchers
A mask that filters sensitive data
A tool for image segmentation
quiz.explanation: The attention mask prevents self-attention heads from wasting computational score mass or contaminating representations with meaningless padding tokens.

quiz.question: What is the difference between extractive summarization and abstractive summarization?
options: Extractive summarization selects and concatenates verbatim sentences directly from the source; abstractive summarization generates original paraphrased text
Extractive uses deep learning; abstractive uses regex
Abstractive only works on bullet points
They produce identical outputs
quiz.explanation: Extractive methods rank and copy source sentences; abstractive methods read the source into latent representations and compose new summary sentences.

quiz.question: What is Named Entity Recognition (NER)?
options: An information extraction task that classifies token spans into predefined categories such as Person, Organization, Location, or Date
Naming Python variables automatically
Recognizing usernames on a network
A classification of GPU hardware models
quiz.explanation: NER identifies real-world entities in text sequences, typically formulated as a token-level classification task using BIO (Beginning, Inside, Outside) tagging.

quiz.question: What is Part-of-Speech (POS) Tagging?
options: Assigning grammatical categories (such as noun, verb, adjective, preposition) to each individual token in a sentence
Tagging posts on social media
Position encoding of tokens
Sorting tokens alphabetically
quiz.explanation: POS tagging labels words according to syntactic function within sentence context.

quiz.question: What is Coreference Resolution in NLP?
options: Identifying all expressions in a text that refer to the exact same real-world entity (e.g. linking 'Elon Musk', 'he', and 'the CEO')
Resolving git merge conflicts in NLP code
Correcting spelling errors
Translating pronouns across languages
quiz.explanation: Coreference resolution connects pronoun and entity mentions to their corresponding antecedent referents across long documents.

quiz.question: What is Cosine Similarity between two embedding vectors u and v?
options: The cosine of the angle between them: (u . v) / (||u||_2 * ||v||_2), measuring semantic directional alignment independent of magnitude
The Euclidean distance between their endpoints
The sum of their absolute values
The difference between their norms
quiz.explanation: Cosine similarity bounds similarity to [-1, 1], quantifying directional orientation regardless of vector scale.

quiz.question: What is Cross-Entropy Loss with Per-Token Averaging in language modeling?
options: Loss = - (1/N) * sum_{t=1}^N log P(x_t | x_{<t})
Loss = sum (y - y_hat)^2
Loss = max(0, 1 - y * y_hat)
Loss = (1/N) * sum |y - y_hat|
quiz.explanation: Language models optimize the negative log-likelihood averaged across all target tokens in the batch.

quiz.question: What is the relationship between Cross-Entropy Loss (in nats) and Perplexity?
options: Perplexity = exp(Cross_Entropy_Loss)
Perplexity = 1 / Cross_Entropy_Loss
Perplexity = Cross_Entropy_Loss^2
Perplexity = log(Cross_Entropy_Loss)
quiz.explanation: Perplexity is the base-e exponential of the cross-entropy loss, representing the geometric mean of inverse conditional probabilities.

topics.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation & Vector DBs
topics.description: Dense vs Sparse Retrieval, HNSW, FAISS, Chunking strategies, Re-ranking with Cross-Encoders, and HyDE.

sections.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) & Vector Search
sections.subtitle: Grounding Generative AI on External Knowledge to Eliminate Hallucinations

sections.title: What is Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Lewis et al., 2020)?
sections.text:
Parametric knowledge stored in LLM weights suffers from knowledge cutoffs, hallucination of non-existent facts, and inability to access private proprietary data. **RAG** resolves this by pairing an information retrieval system with a generative model:
1. **Retrieve:** Given user query $q$, search external knowledge bases to find the top-$k$ most relevant text chunks $\{d_1, \dots, d_k\}$.
2. **Augment:** Construct a context-rich prompt: $\text{Prompt} = [\text{SystemInstructions}, d_1, \dots, d_k, q]$.
3. **Generate:** The LLM generates an answer grounded strictly on the retrieved context.

sections.title: Retrieval Paradigms: Sparse vs Dense vs Hybrid
rows: Sparse (Lexical)
Exact keyword matching via inverted indices and Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency.
High precision on domain-specific codes, part numbers, exact acronyms, and product IDs.
Vulnerable to vocabulary mismatch (synonyms: 'automobile' vs 'car').
BM25, TF-IDF, Elasticsearch, SPLADE.
Dense (Semantic)
Deep bi-encoders project text into continuous semantic vector embeddings; computes cosine/dot-product distance.
Understands conceptual intent, synonyms, and multilingual semantics.
Can miss exact alphanumeric part numbers; computationally heavier.
OpenAI text-embedding-3, BGE, E5, Cohere Embed.
Hybrid Retrieval
Combines sparse (BM25) and dense retrieval scores using **Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)**.
Best of both worlds: robust keyword matching and deep semantic understanding.
Requires managing two search indices concurrently.
Pinecone Hybrid, Weaviate, Qdrant, Elasticsearch.

sections.title: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) Formula
sections.text:
Given rankings from multiple retrievers $R \in \mathcal{R}$ for document $d$, RRF calculates a combined score:

$$\text{RRF}(d) = \sum_{R \in \mathcal{R}} \frac{1}{k + \text{rank}_R(d)}$$

Where $k$ is a constant (typically $k=60$) that prevents top-ranked items from drowning out consistent runners-up across systems.

sections.title: Vector Indexing Algorithms: Flat vs IVF vs HNSW
sections.body:
- **Flat Index:** Exact brute-force $O(N)$ comparison against all $N$ vectors. 100% recall, but completely unscalable beyond $100,000$ vectors.
- **Inverted File (IVF):** Partitions vector space into Voronoi cells via k-means. Queries search only the nearest centroids and their associated inverted lists.
- **Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW, Malkov & Yashunin, 2018):** State-of-the-art multi-layer proximity graph. Queries enter at a sparse top layer and greedily zoom into fine-grained local neighborhoods in $O(\log N)$ time.

sections.title: Two-Stage Retrieval with Cross-Encoder Re-Ranking
sections.text:
1. **Stage 1 (Bi-Encoder Retrieval):** Fast vector search retrieves candidate pool of top-50 documents in $<15\text{ms}$.
2. **Stage 2 (Cross-Encoder Re-Ranker):** Concatenates $[\text{query}, d_i]$ and passes it through a deep bidirectional Transformer with full cross-attention. Ranks top-50 candidates with high precision down to the top-5 documents fed to the LLM.

code_example.title: Minimal In-Memory RAG System with Vector Search in NumPy
code_example.code:
import numpy as np

# Simulated embedding function (producing normalized 4D vectors)
def mock_embed(text):
    np.random.seed(abs(hash(text)) % (2**32))
    v = np.random.randn(4)
    return v / np.linalg.norm(v)

# Knowledge Base documents
corpus = [
    'FastAPI is a modern, fast web framework for building APIs with Python 3.8+.',
    'Convolutional neural networks excel at extracting 2D spatial features from images.',
    'Retrieval-Augmented Generation combines external document retrieval with LLMs to reduce hallucination.',
    'Gradient descent updates weights in the opposite direction of the loss gradient.'
]

# Build vector index
index = np.array([mock_embed(doc) for doc in corpus])

# Query
query = 'How to stop LLM hallucinations using external documents?'
q_vec = mock_embed(query)

# Cosine similarity search (dot product of unit vectors)
similarities = np.dot(index, q_vec)
top_idx = np.argmax(similarities)

print(f'Query: "{query}"')
print(f'Top Match Score: {similarities[top_idx]:.4f}')
print(f'Retrieved Document: "{corpus[top_idx]}"')

# Construct Grounded Prompt
prompt = f'''Context:\n{corpus[top_idx]}\n\nQuestion: {query}\nAnswer based ONLY on the context above:'''
print('\n=== Constructed Grounded Prompt ===\n' + prompt)

quiz.question: What is the primary motivation for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)?
options: Grounding LLM outputs in verified external knowledge to reduce hallucinations, provide citations, and access proprietary data without full retraining
To train smaller models from scratch
To speed up Python code execution
To eliminate the need for vector databases
quiz.explanation: RAG connects LLMs to external dynamic databases, grounding responses in retrieved evidence to eliminate hallucinations and knowledge obsolescence.

quiz.question: What is the fundamental difference between a Bi-Encoder and a Cross-Encoder?
options: A Bi-Encoder embeds queries and documents into vectors independently for fast search; a Cross-Encoder processes (query, doc) pairs jointly through full cross-attention
Bi-Encoders have two GPUs; Cross-Encoders have one
Bi-Encoders only work on images
Cross-Encoders cannot compute similarity
quiz.explanation: Bi-encoders produce decoupled vector representations for ultra-fast ANN search; cross-encoders compute deep query-document cross-attention for high-precision re-ranking.

quiz.question: Why cannot Cross-Encoders be used for Stage 1 initial retrieval over millions of documents?
options: Evaluating a Cross-Encoder requires running the heavy Transformer model for every single document in the database, which is computationally intractable for millions of docs
Cross-Encoders cannot run on GPUs
Cross-Encoders only output binary numbers
Cross-Encoders require unlabelled data
quiz.explanation: Comparing a query against 1 million documents with a Cross-Encoder would require 1 million full forward passes, causing unacceptable latency.

quiz.question: What is Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW)?
options: A graph-based approximate nearest neighbor algorithm that organizes vectors into a hierarchy of proximity graphs for logarithmic-time search
A neural network that navigates small worlds
A routing protocol for smart homes
A compression format for video
quiz.explanation: HNSW structures vectors into multi-layer skip-list graphs, enabling logarithmic O(log N) approximate nearest neighbor search with exceptional recall.

quiz.question: What is Inverted File with Product Quantization (IVF-PQ)?
options: A vector indexing method that clusters vectors into Voronoi cells and compresses high-dimensional vectors into short byte codes to slash RAM usage
An image search algorithm for inverted colors
A method for training neural networks backwards
A file system for storing PDFs
quiz.explanation: IVF-PQ partitions the space with k-means and compresses residual vectors via product quantization, reducing memory footprint by up to 95%.

quiz.question: What is the difference between Cosine Similarity and Dot Product for normalized vectors?
options: They are mathematically identical: if vectors have unit L2 norm (||u|| = 1), cosine similarity equals their dot product
Cosine similarity is always negative
Dot product requires square matrices
Cosine similarity ignores the angle
quiz.explanation: When vectors are L2-normalized to unit length, cosine(u, v) = (u . v) / (1 * 1) = u . v.

quiz.question: What is the BM25 algorithm?
options: A probabilistic sparse retrieval algorithm based on TF-IDF that incorporates document length normalization and term frequency saturation
A neural network architecture with 25 layers
A benchmark for 25 large models
A compression format for text
quiz.explanation: BM25 (Best Matching 25) is the industry-standard lexical keyword ranking algorithm used in search engines like Lucene and Elasticsearch.

quiz.question: What is Vocabulary Mismatch in information retrieval?
options: When a user query uses different words from a document even though they mean the same concept (e.g. 'automobile repair' vs 'car fixing')
When the tokenizer runs out of memory
When text has spelling mistakes
When a foreign language is used
quiz.explanation: Sparse lexical search fails when synonyms differ; dense vector embeddings overcome vocabulary mismatch by embedding semantic meaning.

quiz.question: What is Hybrid Search in modern RAG systems?
options: Combining sparse lexical retrieval (BM25) with dense semantic vector search to capture both exact keyword matches and conceptual intent
Searching across both audio and video
Using both CPU and GPU for search
Searching two different websites simultaneously
quiz.explanation: Hybrid search leverages BM25 for precise keywords (acronyms, serial numbers) and dense embeddings for semantic context, merging rankings.

quiz.question: What is Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)?
options: An algorithm that merges ranked lists from different retrieval systems by summing reciprocal rank scores: sum 1 / (k + rank_i)
A method for fusing two neural networks
A technique for nuclear fusion simulations
A sorting algorithm for integers
quiz.explanation: RRF combines multiple ranked lists without needing score calibration, stably rewarding documents ranked highly across multiple retrievers.

quiz.question: Why is Chunking necessary before indexing documents for RAG?
options: Documents are too large to fit effectively into embedding models and LLM context windows; chunking splits text into coherent, semantically focused passages
Because vector databases can only store 10 words per file
To delete punctuation marks
To hide private data
quiz.explanation: Chunking breaks lengthy documents into granular passages (e.g. 256-512 tokens), preserving local semantic specificity for accurate retrieval.

quiz.question: What is 'Chunk Overlap' and why is it used?
options: Retaining a small percentage (e.g. 10-20%) of shared tokens between consecutive chunks to prevent contextual fractures at boundary seams
Duplicating all documents twice
Overlapping vector database indices across servers
A memory leak in text processing
quiz.explanation: Chunk overlap ensures that sentences crossing chunk boundaries are not split in half, preserving semantic continuity.

quiz.question: What is Semantic Chunking?
options: Splitting text dynamically at points where the semantic distance between adjacent sentence embeddings exceeds a threshold, rather than at fixed character counts
Splitting text by alphabet letters
Cutting paragraphs in half
Chunking based on file size
quiz.explanation: Semantic chunking monitors cosine distance between consecutive sentences, creating chunk boundaries only when topics shift significantly.

quiz.question: What is Parent-Child (Hierarchical) Chunking?
options: Indexing small child chunks for granular vector search, but retrieving the surrounding larger parent chunk to provide complete context to the LLM
Chunking files into folders and subfolders
A method for training child neural networks
A model that inherits from another model
quiz.explanation: Small child chunks produce sharp, accurate embedding matches, while passing the broader parent chunk to the LLM provides sufficient context for generation.

quiz.question: What is Hypothetical Document Embeddings (HyDE, Gao et al., 2022)?
options: Using an LLM to generate a hypothetical answer to the query, then embedding that hypothetical document to search for real documents with similar content
Searching for documents that do not exist
A loss function for embeddings
A method for generating false data
quiz.explanation: HyDE transforms an uninformative short query into a rich, hypothetical document vector that matches the embedding manifold of real corpus passages.

quiz.question: What is 'Lost in the Middle' phenomenon (Liu et al., 2023) in long-context LLMs?
options: LLMs recall information located at the very beginning or end of long context prompts significantly better than information buried in the middle
LLMs crashing when reading 100 pages
Tokens being randomly deleted during inference
Attention weights becoming zero in the middle of a sentence
quiz.explanation: Empirical benchmarks prove that language models exhibit a U-shaped performance curve, frequently failing to retrieve facts located in the middle third of context windows.

quiz.question: How can Re-ranking mitigate the 'Lost in the Middle' problem?
options: By sorting the most critical retrieved documents to the very top and very bottom of the context prompt
By deleting all middle documents
By reversing the entire prompt
By training with larger learning rates
quiz.explanation: Cross-encoder re-ranking surfaces the most relevant passages and places them at the beginning (or ends) where the model's attention is sharpest.

quiz.question: What is Self-RAG (Asai et al., 2023)?
options: A framework where an LLM dynamically decides when to retrieve, evaluates the relevance of retrieved passages, and critiques its own generated output via reflection tokens
A RAG system running on a local laptop
A model that writes its own code
A vector database that updates itself
quiz.explanation: Self-RAG trains models with specialized critique tokens (`[Retrieve]`, `[IsRel]`, `[IsSup]`) to retrieve adaptively and verify answer faithfulness.

quiz.question: What is Corrective RAG (CRAG, Yan et al., 2024)?
options: A framework that evaluates retrieval quality with a lightweight evaluator: if confidence is high, it refines documents; if low, it falls back to web search
Correcting grammar errors in prompts
A spellchecker for vector databases
A method for fixing broken embeddings
quiz.explanation: CRAG assesses retrieval confidence and triggers alternative retrieval pathways (like external web search) when local corpus retrieval is deemed poor.

quiz.question: What is Sentence-Window Retrieval?
options: Embedding individual sentences for precise search, but replacing the retrieved sentence with a surrounding window of k sentences before prompt injection
Opening a sentence in a new desktop window
Splitting sentences by punctuation
A sliding window attention mechanism
quiz.explanation: Sentence-window retrieval matches single sentences for pinpoint precision, while surrounding window context provides necessary paragraph nuance.

quiz.question: What is Multi-Query Retrieval (Query Expansion)?
options: Using an LLM to generate multiple alternative phrasings and perspectives of the user query, executing searches for all of them, and pooling results
Running 10 queries on Google
Searching with multiple users at once
A SQL JOIN operation
quiz.explanation: Multi-query expansion overcomes prompt phrasing limitations by querying the vector store from multiple conceptual angles and taking the union of top results.

quiz.question: What is Contextual Compression in RAG?
options: Extracting only the specific sentences or spans within a retrieved document that are relevant to the query, discarding irrelevant background filler
Compressing documents using Gzip before sending to LLM
Quantizing text to 8-bit characters
Summarizing documents into 1 word
quiz.explanation: Contextual compression extracts only the salient facts from retrieved passages, minimizing token count and reducing context clutter.

quiz.question: What is RAG Triad of Metrics (TruLens / Ragas)?
options: Context Relevance, Groundedness (Faithfulness), and Answer Relevance
Precision, Recall, and F1 Score
Latency, Throughput, and VRAM
Accuracy, Loss, and Perplexity
quiz.explanation: The RAG evaluation triad measures: 1. Did we retrieve relevant context? 2. Is the answer supported by context? 3. Does the answer address the question?

quiz.question: What does 'Faithfulness' measure in RAG evaluation?
options: The extent to which all claims in the generated response can be directly inferred from the provided context passages
How much the user trusts the system
Whether the model uses correct grammar
The uptime of the API server
quiz.explanation: Faithfulness measures the absence of hallucinations by verifying that all generated statements are grounded in retrieved evidence.

quiz.question: What is Context Recall in RAG evaluation?
options: The extent to which all necessary information required to answer the question was successfully retrieved in the context
The speed of the vector index
The memory size of the index
The number of chunks retrieved
quiz.explanation: Context recall evaluates whether the retriever brought back all relevant facts present in the ground-truth reference answer.

quiz.question: What is an Inverted Index in information retrieval?
options: A data structure mapping each unique word to the list of documents and positions where that word occurs
An index stored in reverse alphabetical order
An index that inverts pixel values
A database that reads from bottom to top
quiz.explanation: Inverted indices allow instant O(1) keyword lookups by mapping tokens to postings lists of document IDs.

quiz.question: What is Metadata Filtering in Vector Databases?
options: Filtering vectors by scalar metadata attributes (e.g. `user_id == '123' AND date >= 2024`) before or during approximate nearest neighbor search
Deleting corrupted vector files
Filtering out stopwords from metadata
Renaming database columns
quiz.explanation: Metadata filtering restricts vector search to authorized or relevant subsets based on structured relational tags.

quiz.question: What is the difference between Pre-Filtering and Post-Filtering in vector databases?
options: Pre-filtering applies metadata constraints before vector similarity calculation; post-filtering searches the whole vector space first and discards matches that fail metadata rules
Pre-filtering is only for text; post-filtering is for images
Post-filtering runs on CPUs; pre-filtering on GPUs
They are identical in performance
quiz.explanation: Pre-filtering guarantees metadata criteria are satisfied and restricts the search scope; post-filtering can return zero results if top vector matches all fail metadata checks.

quiz.question: What is ColBERT (Khattab & Zaharia, 2020)?
options: A late-interaction retrieval model that computes token-level vector representations and computes maximum similarity scores via MaxSim: sum_q max_d (q . d)
A model that translates between English and French
A sparse retrieval model based on BM25
A video retrieval architecture
quiz.explanation: ColBERT preserves rich token-level contextual embeddings while retaining near-bi-encoder search speed via efficient MaxSim matrix operations.

quiz.question: What is SPLADE (Formal et al., 2021)?
options: A neural sparse retrieval model that uses a masked language model to expand queries and documents into rich, sparse lexical representations over vocabulary tokens
A vector database written in Rust
A chunking library for PDFs
A method for splitting datasets
quiz.explanation: SPLADE learns sparse lexical representations with automatic term expansion, outperforming BM25 while executing on traditional inverted index engines.

quiz.question: What is GraphRAG (Edge et al., Microsoft 2024)?
options: Extracting knowledge graphs (entities, relations, claims) from raw text with an LLM and using community detection summaries to answer global corpus-wide questions
A RAG system for social networks only
Plotting RAG metrics on a graph
A database using graph neural networks for image search
quiz.explanation: GraphRAG builds structured knowledge graphs from unstructured text, enabling holistic answers to broad questions like 'What are the main themes of this entire corpus?'

quiz.question: What is the impact of embedding dimension on vector database memory?
options: A 1536-dimensional float32 vector requires 6,144 bytes per vector; 1 million vectors consume ~6 GB of RAM just for raw vector data
Embedding dimension has zero impact on memory
Higher dimension always uses less memory
Vectors are stored as 1-bit integers
quiz.explanation: Memory scales linearly with vector dimension: dim * 4 bytes per vector (e.g. 1536 * 4 = 6.144 KB per vector).

quiz.question: What is Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL, Kusupati et al., 2022)?
options: Training embedding models so that the first d dimensions (e.g. 256 of 1024) form valid, high-performing embeddings, allowing flexible dimension truncation to save 75% memory
An embedding model developed in Russia
A model with nested recursive layers
A technique for stacking doll images
quiz.explanation: MRL enforces information density into early dimensions, enabling practitioners to truncate vectors (e.g. 1536 -> 512) with negligible loss in retrieval recall.

quiz.question: What is Distance Metric selection in vector search (Euclidean L2 vs Cosine vs Inner Product)?
options: If vectors are L2-normalized, Cosine Similarity, Inner Product, and Euclidean distance produce identical ranking orders
Inner Product only works on integers
Cosine distance is non-linear
Euclidean distance cannot run on GPUs
quiz.explanation: For unit-normalized vectors: ||u - v||^2 = 2 - 2*(u . v). Thus, ranking by minimum Euclidean distance is mathematically identical to ranking by maximum dot product or cosine.

quiz.question: What is 'Chunk Size' optimization trade-off in RAG?
options: Small chunks capture specific facts but lack context; large chunks preserve complete context but dilute semantic specificity and fill LLM context budgets
Small chunks take longer to embed
Large chunks cannot be stored in databases
Chunk size has no effect on retrieval
quiz.explanation: Tuning chunk size (typically 256-1024 tokens) balances pinpoint search relevance against broad context sufficiency.

topics.title: LLM Fine-Tuning & Alignment (LoRA & DPO)
topics.description: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT: LoRA, QLoRA), and Alignment (RLHF vs DPO).

sections.title: LLM Adaptation, PEFT & Preference Alignment
sections.subtitle: Transforming Raw Base Foundation Models into Aligned, Specialized Assistants

sections.title: The Post-Pretraining Journey
sections.text:
Raw base foundation models (e.g., Llama-3-8B-Base) are trained purely for next-token continuation over trillions of web tokens. Turning them into reliable assistants involves two critical post-training phases:
1. **Instruction Tuning / SFT (Supervised Fine-Tuning):** Teaches the model conversational interaction patterns, formatting compliance, and tool-use syntax.
2. **Preference Alignment (RLHF / DPO):** Aligns outputs with human values of **Helpfulness, Honesty, and Harmlessness (HHH)**.

sections.title: LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation (Hu et al., Microsoft 2021)
sections.text:
Full fine-tuning updates the entire parameter matrix $W_0 \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times k}$. **LoRA** hypothesizes that weight changes $\Delta W$ have a low **intrinsic rank** $r \ll \min(d, k)$. It freezes $W_0$ and decomposes updates into two low-rank matrices:

$$W = W_0 + \Delta W = W_0 + \frac{\alpha}{r} (B \cdot A)$$

Where $A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times k}$ is initialized with Gaussian noise $\mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$, $B \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r}$ is initialized to zero, and $\alpha$ is a constant scaling hyperparameter.

- **Zero Inference Latency:** During deployment, $B \cdot A$ is mathematically added directly to $W_0$, introducing zero latency overhead!
- **VRAM Savings:** For $r=8$ or $16$, trainable parameters drop by **$99.9\%$**, slashing optimizer VRAM requirements.

sections.title: Evolution of LLM Alignment Paradigms
rows: RLHF (PPO)
Train a Reward Model $R(x, y)$ on human pairwise rankings; optimize policy $\pi_\theta$ via Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with a KL divergence penalty to reference model $\pi_{ref}$.
Gold standard for nuanced human preference; powerful exploration.
Extremely complex pipeline: requires maintaining 4 models concurrently in VRAM (Actor, Critic, Reference, Reward).
Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)
Mathematically proves that the constrained RL objective can be reparameterized to express the reward directly in terms of policy probability ratios $\frac{\pi_\theta(y|x)}{\pi_{ref}(y|x)}$.
Requires NO reward model and NO reinforcement learning loop; stable supervised loss.
Sensitive to noisy preference labels; susceptible to likelihood displacement on out-of-distribution prompts.
Kahneman-Tversky Optimization (KTO)
Aligns models directly on binary signals (thumbs up / thumbs down) using Prospect Theory utility functions.
Eliminates the need for paired $(y_{win}, y_{lose})$ data; works on cheaper unpaired feedback.
Slightly less sample efficient on subtle ranking nuances.

sections.title: QLoRA: Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation (Dettmers et al., 2023)
sections.text:
**QLoRA** enables fine-tuning a 70B parameter model on a single 48GB GPU by combining:
1. **4-bit NormalFloat (NF4):** Information-theoretically optimal quantile quantization for normally distributed weights.
2. **Double Quantization (DQ):** Quantizes the quantization constants themselves, saving $0.37$ bits per parameter.
3. **Paged Optimizers:** Uses CUDA Unified Memory to automatically page optimizer states to CPU RAM during memory spikes.

code_example.title: LoRA Linear Layer Forward and Merge in NumPy
code_example.code:
import numpy as np

class LoRALinear:
    def __init__(self, in_features, out_features, rank=4, lora_alpha=16):
        self.in_features = in_features
        self.out_features = out_features
        self.rank = rank
        self.scaling = lora_alpha / rank
        
        # Frozen base weights (simulating 8B parameter weights)
        self.W0 = np.random.randn(out_features, in_features) * 0.02
        self.W0_frozen = True
        
        # Trainable low-rank adapter matrices
        self.A = np.random.randn(rank, in_features) * 0.01  # Gaussian init
        self.B = np.zeros((out_features, rank))             # Zero init so delta starts at 0
        
    def forward(self, x):
        # Base output + scaled low-rank output
        base_out = np.dot(x, self.W0.T)
        lora_out = np.dot(np.dot(x, self.A.T), self.B.T) * self.scaling
        return base_out + lora_out
        
    def merge_weights_for_inference(self):
        # Permanently fold delta into W0: Zero inference latency overhead!
        self.W0 += (np.dot(self.B, self.A) * self.scaling)
        self.B = None
        self.A = None
        print('LoRA successfully merged into base weights!')

# Instantiate layer: 4096 -> 4096 with rank r=8
layer = LoRALinear(in_features=4096, out_features=4096, rank=8, lora_alpha=16)
x = np.random.randn(2, 4096)
y_before = layer.forward(x)

# Mock training step updating B
layer.B += np.random.randn(4096, 8) * 0.05
y_after = layer.forward(x)
print(f'Difference in output after adapter update: {np.linalg.norm(y_after - y_before):.4f}')

# Merge for production serving
layer.merge_weights_for_inference()
y_merged = np.dot(x, layer.W0.T)
print(f'Max difference between merged W0 and adapter forward pass: {np.max(np.abs(y_merged - y_after)):.2e}')

quiz.question: What is the primary difference between a Base foundation model and an Instruct/Chat model?
options: Base models are pretrained purely for next-token prediction; Instruct models undergo supervised fine-tuning and alignment to follow user conversational instructions
Base models have fewer parameters
Instruct models cannot generate code
Base models run only on CPUs
quiz.explanation: Base models predict raw text continuations (and often complete user prompts with more questions); Instruct models are fine-tuned to answer prompts helpfully.

quiz.question: What is Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) in the LLM post-training pipeline?
options: Training the pretrained model on curated (prompt, response) instruction demonstrations using standard causal cross-entropy loss
Fine-tuning without labels
Training the tokenizer on code
Running reinforcement learning with human feedback
quiz.explanation: SFT fine-tunes the base model on high-quality demonstration dialogues, teaching it to respond as an assistant rather than just continuing raw text.

quiz.question: What hypothesis underpins Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA, Hu et al., 2021)?
options: The weight updates Delta W during task adaptation have a very low intrinsic dimension / rank r relative to the full weight dimension
Weights in deep models are all identical
Models only need 1 layer to learn
Rank cannot exceed 2
quiz.explanation: Hu et al. demonstrated that fine-tuning adaptation changes reside in a very low-dimensional subspace (intrinsic rank r << d), enabling low-rank decomposition.

quiz.question: In LoRA, how is the adapter matrix B initialized, and why?
options: Initialized to all zeros, ensuring that at step 0 the adaptation Delta W = B * A is exactly zero, leaving pretrained behavior unaffected
Initialized to random Gaussian noise
Initialized to all ones
Initialized with identity matrix
quiz.explanation: Initializing B to zero ensures Delta W = 0 initially, meaning the model's forward pass begins exactly identically to the pretrained foundation model.

quiz.question: In LoRA, how is the adapter matrix A initialized?
options: Initialized with random Gaussian values N(0, sigma^2) to break symmetry
Initialized to all zeros
Initialized to all negative numbers
Initialized with the identity matrix
quiz.explanation: Matrix A is initialized randomly from a Gaussian distribution to break symmetry, while B=0 ensures initial product B*A = 0.

quiz.question: What is the primary inference latency advantage of LoRA over other adapter methods?
options: LoRA weights can be folded (merged) directly into the frozen base weights via W = W0 + (alpha/r)*B*A, adding zero additional computation or latency at inference
LoRA cuts inference time by 10x
LoRA eliminates the tokenizer
LoRA runs without GPUs
quiz.explanation: Because matrix multiplication is linear, B*A can be precomputed and added directly to W0 before deploying, introducing zero runtime latency penalty.

quiz.question: Why does LoRA drastically reduce GPU VRAM requirements during training?
options: It freezes the massive base model and only stores gradients and optimizer states (Adam moments) for the tiny r x d matrices, saving up to 75% VRAM
It converts the model to a decision tree
It deletes half the layers
It moves all tensors to CPU disk
quiz.explanation: Optimizer states (Adam requires 8 bytes per trainable parameter) dominate training VRAM; reducing trainable parameters by 99% eliminates optimizer memory overhead.

quiz.question: What is QLoRA (Dettmers et al., 2023)?
options: Quantizing the frozen base model to 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4) while training 16-bit LoRA adapters on top, enabling fine-tuning of 70B models on a single 48GB GPU
A model that runs on quantum computers
A 1-bit neural network
A library for SQL queries
quiz.explanation: QLoRA combines NF4 4-bit base weight quantization with Double Quantization and Paged Optimizers to fine-tune massive LLMs on consumer GPUs.

quiz.question: What is the 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4) data type in QLoRA?
options: An information-theoretically optimal quantile quantization scheme where each bin contains an equal number of expected values for normally distributed weights
A standard IEEE 754 float
An integer with 4 bits
A floating point with 4 exponent bits and 0 mantissa
quiz.explanation: Since pretrained weights naturally follow a zero-mean normal distribution, NF4 spaces quantization bins so that each bin has equal probability under N(0, 1).

quiz.question: What is Double Quantization in QLoRA?
options: Quantizing the quantization scaling constants themselves from FP32 to FP8, saving approximately 0.37 bits per parameter
Quantizing the model twice
Using two 4-bit GPUs
Multiplying weights by 2
quiz.explanation: Double quantization reduces the memory footprint of the quantization scale factors by compressing them into 8-bit floats.

quiz.question: What is the HHH alignment criterion defined by Anthropic?
options: Helpful, Honest, and Harmless
High-throughput, High-accuracy, and High-speed
Hierarchical, Heuristic, and Holistic
Hybrid, Heterogeneous, and Hardware-accelerated
quiz.explanation: The HHH framework sets the standard safety alignment targets: helpful to user queries, honest/truthful without fabrication, and harmless/non-toxic.

quiz.question: What are the four models concurrently maintained in GPU memory during standard RLHF with PPO?
options: Actor (policy being updated), Critic (value function), Reference model (frozen baseline), and Reward model
Student, Teacher, Assistant, and Proctor
Encoder, Decoder, Classifier, and Discriminator
Four identical copies of GPT-4
quiz.explanation: PPO requires: 1. Actor (generating tokens), 2. Critic (estimating state values), 3. Reference model (computing KL penalty), 4. Reward model (scoring output quality).

quiz.question: What is the purpose of the KL divergence penalty in the RLHF PPO objective?
options: To prevent the policy model from drifting too far from the original reference model and collapsing into gibberish or adversarial reward hacking
To calculate learning rate
To compress weights
To speed up generation
quiz.explanation: Without the KL penalty, the policy exploits imperfections in the reward model ('reward hacking') and degrades conversational fluency.

quiz.question: What is Reward Hacking in reinforcement learning from human feedback?
options: When the policy discovers degenerate token sequences or superficial patterns (e.g. excessively long text or repetitive sycophancy) that achieve high reward without truly being good
Hacking into a cloud server to steal rewards
Using an unauthorized credit card for API calls
A hardware fault in GPU registers
quiz.explanation: Reward models are imperfect proxies; unconstrained RL policies learn to exploit these flaws rather than truly satisfying user intent.

quiz.question: What is Direct Preference Optimization (DPO, Rafailov et al., Stanford 2023)?
options: An alignment algorithm that reparameterizes the RL objective to optimize the policy directly on preference pairs (y_win, y_lose) via supervised loss without an explicit reward model or RL loop
A direct search algorithm for hyperparameter optimization
A method for directly training without data
A tool for directing traffic on network switches
quiz.explanation: DPO analytically solves the optimal reward formulation in terms of the policy itself, replacing complex PPO loops with a stable, closed-form cross-entropy loss.

quiz.question: What is the mathematical form of the DPO loss for preference pair (x, y_w, y_l)?
options: - log sigma( beta * log( pi_theta(y_w|x) / pi_ref(y_w|x) ) - beta * log( pi_theta(y_l|x) / pi_ref(y_l|x) ) )
Loss = (y_w - y_l)^2
Loss = max(0, 1 - y_w + y_l)
Loss = - y_w * log(y_l)
quiz.explanation: DPO computes the implicit reward difference between the winning and losing response relative to the reference model, squashed through a sigmoid function.

quiz.question: What is Kahneman-Tversky Optimization (KTO, Ethayarajh et al., 2024)?
options: An alignment method inspired by behavioral economics (Prospect Theory) that optimizes models directly from binary feedback (desirable vs undesirable) without requiring paired preferences
A game theory algorithm for chess
A theory of cognitive psychology for humans only
A loss function for linear regression
quiz.explanation: KTO aligns models on individual thumbs-up / thumbs-down ratings using utility functions that model human loss aversion, avoiding costly pairwise ranking annotations.

quiz.question: What is Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback (RLAIF / Constitutional AI, Anthropic 2022)?
options: Using a strong LLM to critique and score responses based on a defined set of constitutional principles, replacing human annotators in alignment
Training an AI to play video games
Using neural networks to grade student exams
A computer chip designed for AI feedback
